        <title type="text">Is there a modular-invariant, locally generated, finite-index subalgebra of a half-line algebra that does not come from a subnet?</title>
            <category scheme="https://mathoverflow.net/tags" term="oa.operator-algebras" />
            <category scheme="https://mathoverflow.net/tags" term="mp.mathematical-physics" />
            <category scheme="https://mathoverflow.net/tags" term="quantum-field-theory" />
        <author>
            <name>Michael Roeseler</name>
            <uri>https://mathoverflow.net/users/601726</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://mathoverflow.net/questions/516423/is-there-a-modular-invariant-locally-generated-finite-index-subalgebra-of-a-ha" />
        <published>2026-10-26T18:49:50Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-26T18:49:50Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>I am looking at a structural property of subnets in algebraic QFT: whether a single
inclusion that is well-behaved with respect to the vacuum modular flow is forced to
look like a finite-index subnet locally. I have a construction that I believe shows
it is not, and I would like to know whether the construction is correct, and whether
this is already known.</p>
<p><strong>Setting.</strong> Let <span class="math-container">$\{\mathcal A(I)\}$</span> be a translation–dilation covariant chiral net
on <span class="math-container">$\mathbb R$</span> with vacuum <span class="math-container">$\Omega$</span>, and let <span class="math-container">$\mathcal M=\mathcal A(\mathbb R_+)$</span>, so
that <span class="math-container">$\Omega$</span> is cyclic and separating for <span class="math-container">$\mathcal M$</span> and, by Bisognano–Wichmann,
<span class="math-container">$\sigma_t^\Omega$</span> is the dilation group. Let <span class="math-container">$\mathcal K$</span> denote the bounded open
intervals <span class="math-container">$J$</span> with <span class="math-container">$\overline J\subset(0,\infty)$</span>. Suppose a von Neumann subalgebra
<span class="math-container">$\mathcal N\subseteq\mathcal M$</span> satisfies:</p>
<ol>
<li><strong>Modular invariance.</strong> <span class="math-container">$\sigma_t^\Omega(\mathcal N)=\mathcal N$</span> for all <span class="math-container">$t$</span>; by
Takesaki's theorem there is a unique <span class="math-container">$\Omega$</span>-preserving normal conditional
expectation <span class="math-container">$E:\mathcal M\to\mathcal N$</span>.</li>
<li><strong>Local generation.</strong> <span class="math-container">$\mathcal N=\bigvee_{J\in\mathcal K}\big(\mathcal N\cap\mathcal A(J)\big)$</span>.</li>
<li><strong>Finite index.</strong> <span class="math-container">$1&lt;\operatorname{Ind}(E)&lt;\infty$</span> (Kosaki index).</li>
</ol>
<p>Write <span class="math-container">$\mathcal N(J)=\mathcal N\cap\mathcal A(J)$</span>. The natural hope is that
<span class="math-container">$J\mapsto\mathcal N(J)$</span> is then a translation-covariant subnet, so that by
Longo–Rehren it is classified by a Q-system. Covariance would also give the local
statements for free: <span class="math-container">$\mathcal N(J)$</span> would be invariant under the modular group of
<span class="math-container">$(\mathcal A(J),\Omega)$</span>, which is geometric, and the local index would be
independent of <span class="math-container">$J$</span>. So everything turns on translation covariance. Condition 1 gives
dilation covariance; nothing obviously gives translations.</p>
<p><strong>Why condition 2 is there.</strong> Condition 1 alone does not suffice. For the
one-flavor free fermion, a <span class="math-container">$\mathbb Z_3$</span> action by a phase on half of the Mellin
variable satisfies 1 and 3, but its fixed-point algebra meets every <span class="math-container">$\mathcal A(J)$</span>
only in the scalars: by Paley–Wiener, no compactly supported vector can be an
eigenvector of a non-constant Mellin multiplier. The same argument suggests that for
one flavor, any quasi-free gauge satisfying 1 and 2 is a constant phase, hence
covariant.</p>
<p><strong>The construction (two flavors).</strong> Take the free complex chiral fermion with
one-particle space <span class="math-container">$L^2(\mathbb R,\mathbb C^2)$</span>, and pass to <span class="math-container">$y=\log x$</span> on the
half-line via <span class="math-container">$f\mapsto e^{y/2}f(e^y)$</span>, so dilations become translations in <span class="math-container">$y$</span>.
Let <span class="math-container">$s$</span> be the Fourier variable dual to <span class="math-container">$y$</span>. The vacuum two-point function restricted
to <span class="math-container">$\mathcal M$</span> is diagonal in <span class="math-container">$s$</span> and scalar in flavor. Put
<span class="math-container">$$A(s)=\operatorname{sinc}^2(s),\qquad B(s)=\operatorname{sinc}^2(\sqrt2\,s),\qquad e(s)=\frac{(A(s),B(s))}{|(A(s),B(s))|},$$</span>
which is well defined because <span class="math-container">$A$</span> and <span class="math-container">$B$</span> have no common real zeros. Let
<span class="math-container">$u=\omega P_{e(s)}+(1-P_{e(s)})$</span> with <span class="math-container">$\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$</span>, a Fourier multiplier in
<span class="math-container">$y$</span>, and let <span class="math-container">$\alpha$</span> be the Bogoliubov automorphism it induces. Take
<span class="math-container">$\mathcal N=\mathcal M^{\langle\alpha\rangle}$</span>.</p>
<ul>
<li><em>Condition 1:</em> <span class="math-container">$u$</span> commutes with translations in <span class="math-container">$y$</span>, i.e. with dilations, and
preserves the restricted vacuum, since the two-point function is scalar in flavor.</li>
<li><em>Condition 3:</em> <span class="math-container">$E=\frac13\sum_k\alpha^k$</span>, so <span class="math-container">$E\ge\frac13\,\mathrm{id}$</span> and
Pimsner–Popa gives <span class="math-container">$1&lt;\operatorname{Ind}(E)\le3$</span>.</li>
<li><em>Condition 2:</em> <span class="math-container">$\hat h=(A,B)$</span> and <span class="math-container">$\hat h'=(-B,A)$</span> are transforms of compactly
supported vectors (triangle functions), with <span class="math-container">$uh=\omega h$</span> and <span class="math-container">$uh'=h'$</span>. Their
translates in <span class="math-container">$y$</span> — dilates on the half-line — lie in <span class="math-container">$L^2(J)$</span> for <span class="math-container">$J\in\mathcal K$</span>,
and since <span class="math-container">$|(A,B)|&gt;0$</span> they span each eigenspace densely (Wiener). Invariant
monomials such as <span class="math-container">$\psi(k)$</span> for <span class="math-container">$uk=k$</span> and <span class="math-container">$\psi(k_1)^*\psi(k_2)$</span> for
<span class="math-container">$uk_i=\omega k_i$</span>, built from these local eigenvectors, lie in <span class="math-container">$\mathcal N(J)$</span>.
I believe they generate <span class="math-container">$\mathcal N$</span>, but I have not carefully checked the passage
from density to generation in the weak operator topology.</li>
<li><em>Covariance fails:</em> <span class="math-container">$u$</span> is a non-constant multiplier in <span class="math-container">$s$</span>, so it does not commute
with translations, and <span class="math-container">$J\mapsto\mathcal N(J)$</span> is not a covariant subnet.</li>
</ul>
<p>The mechanism is that with two flavors the eigenvector direction <span class="math-container">$e(s)$</span> can twist
with <span class="math-container">$s$</span>, and a compactly supported vector-valued function can follow the twist,
which escapes the one-flavor Paley–Wiener obstruction.</p>
<p><strong>Questions.</strong></p>
<ol>
<li>Is this a correct counterexample, in particular condition 2?</li>
<li>Does the stronger local failure also occur, i.e. is <span class="math-container">$\mathcal N(J)$</span> non-invariant
under the modular group of <span class="math-container">$(\mathcal A(J),\Omega)$</span>, or does the local index vary
with <span class="math-container">$J$</span>?</li>
<li>Is positive-translation invariance, <span class="math-container">$U(a)\mathcal N U(a)^*\subseteq\mathcal N$</span> for
<span class="math-container">$a\ge0$</span> (a half-sided modular condition), the natural extra hypothesis that
restores the subnet conclusion?</li>
<li>Is any of this already in the literature? I have looked at Longo–Rehren, Longo's
work on conformal subnets and intermediate subfactors, Carpi–Conti on subsystems,
and Guido–Longo–Wiesbrock, but these start from a net rather than a single
subalgebra.</li>
</ol>
<p>The same question can be asked for a wedge algebra of a Poincaré-covariant net in
Minkowski space, where condition 1 gives boost covariance only. I have only
considered the chiral case.</p>

        </summary>
    </entry>

            <name>prochet</name>

        <link rel="alternate" href="https://mathoverflow.net/questions/516422/a1-connected-components-for-variety-of-maximal-tori" />
        <published>2026-10-26T18:18:33Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-26T18:18:33Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>Let <span class="math-container">$G$</span> be a split group over a field <span class="math-container">$k$</span> of characteristic zero,<span class="math-container">$T$</span> a split maximal torus, <span class="math-container">$N$</span> its normalizer. Then <span class="math-container">$G/T$</span> is <span class="math-container">$\mathbb{A}^1$</span>-connected (in the sense of Morel), as it is <span class="math-container">$\mathbb{A}^1$</span>-homotopic to <span class="math-container">$G/B$</span>, which is rational and smooth projective, thus <span class="math-container">$\mathbb{A}^1$</span>-connected. But apparently, its not the case of <span class="math-container">$G/N$</span>, because in his ICM address (Remark 3.9) Morel states that an <span class="math-container">$\mathbb{A}^{1}$</span>-connected scheme in characteristic zero has no non-trivial finite étale covers.</p>
<p>So what is <span class="math-container">$\pi_{0}^{\mathbb{A}^1}(G/N)$</span> then?</p>

        </summary>

        <title type="text">Simplification of a weight four polylogarithm combination at complex arguments</title>
            <category scheme="https://mathoverflow.net/tags" term="analytic-number-theory" />
            <category scheme="https://mathoverflow.net/tags" term="special-functions" />
            <category scheme="https://mathoverflow.net/tags" term="polylogarithms" />
        <author>
            <name>Faeq</name>
            <uri>https://mathoverflow.net/users/601723</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://mathoverflow.net/questions/516421/simplification-of-a-weight-four-polylogarithm-combination-at-complex-arguments" />
        <published>2026-10-26T16:45:38Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-26T16:45:38Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>Consider the constant:</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$$
S=\frac12\operatorname{Im}\left[
\operatorname{Li}_{3,1}\left(\frac12,1-i\right)
-\operatorname{Li}_{3,1}\left(1,\frac{1-i}{2}\right)
\right]
$$</span></p>
<p>where the multiple polylogarithm is defined by:</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$$
\operatorname{Li}_{a,b}(x,y)
=\sum_{\substack{n&gt;m\\m\ge1}}
\frac{x^n y^m}{n^a m^b}
$$</span></p>
<p>with analytic continuation where necessary.</p>
<p>I am interested in whether <span class="math-container">$S$</span> can be reduced to classical polylogarithms and standard constants, with no multiple polylogarithms remaining.</p>
<ol>
<li>Are there shuffle, stuffle or functional identities that simplify this specific difference?</li>
<li>Can it be expressed as a finite combination of classical polylogarithms <span class="math-container">$\operatorname{Li}_k(z)$</span>, logarithms, zeta values, Dirichlet beta values, and powers of <span class="math-container">$\pi$</span>, preferably evaluated at algebraic arguments?</li>
<li>If such a reduction is not readily available through known identities, are there symbolic algorithms or computer algebra packages suitable for investigating this combination?</li>
</ol>
<p>References to applicable reduction identities or algorithms would be appreciated.</p>

        </summary>

        <published>2026-10-26T13:54:13Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-26T15:29:26Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>A space <span class="math-container">$(X,\tau)$</span> is <em>homogeneous</em> if for all <span class="math-container">$x, y\in X$</span> there is a homeomorphism <span class="math-container">$\varphi: X\to X$</span> such that <span class="math-container">$\varphi(x) = y$</span>.</p>
<p><strong>Question.</strong> Suppose <span class="math-container">$(X, \tau)$</span> is infinite, <span class="math-container">$T_2$</span> and homogeneous, and let <span class="math-container">$x, y \in X$</span> with <span class="math-container">$x\neq y$</span>. Are there disjoint open sets <span class="math-container">$U, V\subseteq X$</span> with <span class="math-container">$x\in U, y\in V$</span> and <span class="math-container">$U\cong V\cong X$</span>?</p>

        <title type="text">Is a pseudoline arrangement in $\mathbb{RP}^2$ determined by its labelled graph?</title>
            <category scheme="https://mathoverflow.net/tags" term="co.combinatorics" />
            <category scheme="https://mathoverflow.net/tags" term="discrete-geometry" />
            <category scheme="https://mathoverflow.net/tags" term="topological-graph-theory" />
        <author>
            <name>Michel Hua</name>
            <uri>https://mathoverflow.net/users/601434</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://mathoverflow.net/questions/516410/is-a-pseudoline-arrangement-in-mathbbrp2-determined-by-its-labelled-graph" />
        <published>2026-10-26T11:09:13Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-26T19:35:13Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>Let <span class="math-container">$A = \{L_1, \dots, L_n\}$</span> be an arrangement of pseudolines in <span class="math-container">$\mathbb{RP}^2$</span>, i.e. simple closed curves any two of which cross exactly once.</p>
<p>Let the labelled graph <span class="math-container">$G(A)$</span> be the graph whose vertices are the crossing points <span class="math-container">$L_i \cap L_j$</span> and whose edges are the segments of each <span class="math-container">$L_i$</span> between consecutive crossings, each edge labelled by the <span class="math-container">$i$</span> of its pseudoline. Assume every <span class="math-container">$L_i$</span> carries at least three crossing points.</p>
<p>Take a graph isomorphism <span class="math-container">$\varphi : G(A) \to G(A')$</span> that respects the labels up to a permutation <span class="math-container">$\sigma$</span>, so edges of <span class="math-container">$L_i$</span> go to edges of <span class="math-container">$L'_{\sigma(i)}$</span>.</p>
<p>Is <span class="math-container">$\varphi$</span> always induced by a homeomorphism <span class="math-container">$h$</span> of <span class="math-container">$\mathbb{RP}^2$</span> with <span class="math-container">$h(L_i) = L'_{\sigma(i)}$</span>? Does the labelled graph determine the drawing, and does every symmetry of the graph come from a symmetry of the drawing?</p>
<p><a href="https://i.sstatic.net/TM7Vk1YJ.png" rel="nofollow noreferrer"><img src="https://i.sstatic.net/TM7Vk1YJ.png" alt="four arrangements" /></a></p>
<p><strong>Sketch of an approach.</strong> Grothendieck states in notes on pseudolines, that knowing which triangles are faces would be enough. For a triangle formed by three lines, a fourth line that avoids its corners can tell, through the order in which it crosses the three sides ; this is Grothendieck's condition (A5). The difficulty is when every other line passes through a corner, as in the complete quadrangle (rightmost picture): for the triangle with sides <span class="math-container">$AB$</span>, <span class="math-container">$BC$</span>, <span class="math-container">$CA$</span>, the remaining lines <span class="math-container">$AD$</span>, <span class="math-container">$BD$</span>, <span class="math-container">$CD$</span> each pass through a corner.</p>
<p>The assumption of three crossings per line rules out arrangements like three lines through <span class="math-container">$P$</span>, two through <span class="math-container">$Q$</span>, plus the line <span class="math-container">$PQ$</span>, which meets the others only at <span class="math-container">$P$</span> and <span class="math-container">$Q$</span>.</p>
<p>He notes that the step behind (A5) is not checked: <em>&quot;Il faudrait, dans cette optique, pour (A5) savoir que ce ψ ne dépend pas des choix arbitraires qui ont été faits […]. Je n'ai donc pas vérifié que la proposition énoncée soit correcte&quot;</em>.</p>
<p>Has this been proved somewhere, or is it false?</p>
<p><strong>Source.</strong> (Montpellier archive, <a href="https://grothendieck.umontpellier.fr/80.pdf" rel="nofollow noreferrer">cote 80</a>, p. 48-54, 1981)</p>

        </summary>
    </entry>

        <title type="text">Second adjacency eigenvalue of Apollonian networks: is $\theta_2(G_m)/2^{m/2} \to \sqrt{2}$?</title>
            <category scheme="https://mathoverflow.net/tags" term="graph-theory" />
            <category scheme="https://mathoverflow.net/tags" term="spectral-graph-theory" />
        <author>
            <name>Rad Sarar Anando</name>
            <uri>https://mathoverflow.net/users/589228</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://mathoverflow.net/questions/516405/second-adjacency-eigenvalue-of-apollonian-networks-is-theta-2g-m-2m-2-t" />
        <published>2026-10-26T06:30:29Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-26T06:30:29Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>Let <span class="math-container">$G_0 = K_4$</span> with outer triangle <span class="math-container">$abc$</span> and central vertex <span class="math-container">$o$</span>. <span class="math-container">$G_m$</span> is obtained from <span class="math-container">$G_{m-1}$</span> by inserting a new vertex into every inner triangular face, joined to its three corners. The outer face <span class="math-container">$abc$</span> is never subdivided. So <span class="math-container">$N_m = (3^{m+1}+5)/2$</span>, <span class="math-container">$\deg a = \deg b = \deg c = 2^{m+1}+1$</span>, and <span class="math-container">$\deg o = 3 \cdot 2^m$</span>. Let <span class="math-container">$\theta_1 \ge \theta_2 \ge \dots$</span> be the adjacency eigenvalues of <span class="math-container">$G_m$</span>.</p>
<p>(For bounds <span class="math-container">$m \ge 8$</span>):</p>
<p><span class="math-container">$$\sqrt{2^{m+1} - m - 2} - 1/2 \le \theta_2(G_m) \le 2\sqrt{2} \cdot 2^{m/2}$$</span></p>
<ol>
<li><strong>Lower bound:</strong> test vectors supported on <span class="math-container">$a$</span> (resp. <span class="math-container">$b$</span>) and its private neighbours, plus the <span class="math-container">$2 \times 2$</span> compression.</li>
<li><strong>Upper bound:</strong> interlacing gives <span class="math-container">$\theta_2(G_m) \le \theta_1(G_m - o)$</span>. Orient edges child <span class="math-container">$\to$</span> parent and apply <span class="math-container">$2x_u x_v \le \beta x_u^2 + x_v^2/\beta$</span> with <span class="math-container">$\beta$</span> depending only on the child's level.</li>
</ol>
<p>For <span class="math-container">$m \le 11$</span>:
<span class="math-container">$\theta_2^2/2^m = 2.684, 2.492, 2.335, 2.225$</span> for <span class="math-container">$m = 8, \dots, 11$</span>, decreasing slowly. <span class="math-container">$\theta_1^2/2^m = 3.77, 3.45, 3.28, 3.18$</span>. This suggests <span class="math-container">$\theta_1^2 \approx \deg o$</span> and <span class="math-container">$\theta_2^2 \approx \deg a$</span>, but it is numerical only.</p>
<p><strong>Question.</strong> Is <span class="math-container">$\lim \theta_2(G_m)/2^{m/2} = \sqrt{2}$</span>? Equivalently, is <span class="math-container">$\limsup \le \sqrt{2}$</span>? Weighted AM–GM with weights depending on the child's level gives only <span class="math-container">$2\sqrt{2}$</span>, and weights depending on both levels numerically gives about <span class="math-container">$2.05$</span>, so I think a genealogy-aware argument is needed. Is the spectrum of <span class="math-container">$G_m$</span> (or of random Apollonian networks, where top eigenvalues follow the square roots of top degrees) known to follow this pattern?</p>

        </summary>

        <title type="text">Independence and approximate independence of random variables</title>
            <category scheme="https://mathoverflow.net/tags" term="pr.probability" />
        <author>
            <name>Brayden</name>
            <uri>https://mathoverflow.net/users/522078</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://mathoverflow.net/questions/516404/independence-and-approximate-independence-of-random-variables" />
        <published>2026-10-26T06:09:07Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-26T06:09:07Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>Let <span class="math-container">$A \in \mathbb{Z}^{n \times N}$</span> be an integer matrix with columns <span class="math-container">$a_1, \ldots, a_N$</span>. Consider its integer kernel <span class="math-container">$K = \ker A \cap \mathbb{Z}^N$</span>. Now, let <span class="math-container">$\theta \sim \mathbb{T}^n$</span> be a (uniformly) random vector on the torus. Consider the following random variables <span class="math-container">$X_j = f_j(a_j \cdot \theta)$</span> for <span class="math-container">$j = 1, \ldots, N$</span> for sufficiently regular functions <span class="math-container">$f_j : \mathbb{T} \to \mathbb{C}$</span> (so that I may not think when I interchange integrals).</p>
<p>Although these random variables I described above are generally dependent, we may write the following beautiful fact, which is immediate from an expansion into Fourier series
<span class="math-container">$$
    \mathbb{E} \prod_{j = 1}^N X_j = \sum_{m \in K} \prod_{j = 1}^N \widehat {f_j}(m_j).
$$</span>
Note that seperating <span class="math-container">$m = 0$</span> gives
<span class="math-container">$$
    \mathbb{E} \prod_{j = 1}^N X_j - \prod_{j = 1}^N \mathbb{E}\, X_j = \sum_{0 \neq m \in K} \prod_{j = 1}^N \widehat {f_j}(m_j),
$$</span>
and so of course we can characterize independence here in terms of the Fourier transforms of the <span class="math-container">$f_j$</span>'s. This is a lovely fact, but I think I'd be crazy to assume that this fact hasn't been completely examined in literature under a well-known set of ideas and in a more general setting. Does anyone know if/where I can find these works? Thanks.</p>

        </summary>

        <title type="text">Is the height factor in a prime-tone model of the Riemann zero gaps a restatement of Bogomolny–Keating's finite-height corrections?</title>
            <category scheme="https://mathoverflow.net/tags" term="nt.number-theory" />
        <author>
            <name>user601687</name>
            <uri>https://mathoverflow.net/users/601687</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://mathoverflow.net/questions/516401/is-the-height-factor-in-a-prime-tone-model-of-the-riemann-zero-gaps-a-restatemen" />
        <published>2026-10-25T23:47:53Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-26T08:58:11Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>I don't know if this is a crazy question,</p>
<p>I have been treating the normalized gaps between consecutive zeros of the Riemann zeta function as a sequence in its own right, with the gap index as time, and measuring how predictable that sequence is at short lags. One piece of the result is a formula I cannot place, and it is the reason for this post.</p>
<p>Terms. The normalized gap at the <span class="math-container">$n$</span>-th zero is the gap <span class="math-container">$\gamma_{n+1} - \gamma_n$</span> multiplied by <span class="math-container">$\log(\gamma_n / 2\pi) / (2\pi)$</span>, so the local mean spacing is 1 at every height. By sequence space I mean the resulting sequence regarded in its index <span class="math-container">$n$</span>. A prime tone is a sinusoid in <span class="math-container">$n$</span> at the frequency <span class="math-container">$f_p = \log p / (2\pi)$</span>. In the height factor <span class="math-container">$(1 + \cos(2T \ln q))/2$</span>, <span class="math-container">$T$</span> is the height of the block of zeros and <span class="math-container">$q$</span> is the prime attached to the tone. The repulsion floor is the predictability the identical pipeline achieves on <span class="math-container">$\beta$</span>-Hermite random-matrix surrogates, which carry the zeros' generic level repulsion and nothing else. The forking-paths count is the number of analysis choices made after seeing the data. AR(20) is an autoregressive model of order 20: each gap predicted from the twenty preceding gaps. Demeaned means the block's mean is subtracted first; held-out means gaps the model was not fitted on; a lag is one step in the index. The surrogates are Dumitriu–Edelman <span class="math-container">$\beta$</span>-Hermite tridiagonal ensembles with <span class="math-container">$\beta$</span> swept over 0.5, 1, and 2, sixty repetitions, unfolded and matched in size to the zero blocks.</p>
<p>When the gap sequence is decomposed into tones at the frequencies <span class="math-container">$\log p / 2\pi$</span>, for the primes up to 29, each tone's amplitude is predicted, with nothing fitted, by the explicit formula's prefactor times a height factor, <span class="math-container">$(1 + \cos(2T \ln q))/2$</span>, that depends on the height <span class="math-container">$T$</span> of the zeros in the block. The law was frozen on the first 699 zeros (<span class="math-container">$T$</span> from 14 to 1063) and then used unchanged to predict the amplitudes on a disjoint block, zeros 2000 to 2699 (<span class="math-container">$T$</span> from 2515 to 3233). The <span class="math-container">$p = 2$</span> tone fell to 0.67 times its low-range amplitude, against a prediction of 0.64, and the <span class="math-container">$p = 29$</span> tone rose to 2.68 times, against a prediction of 3.04. My question is whether this height factor is a change of variables away from the finite-height correction terms in Bogomolny and Keating's work on the pair correlation, or whether it is a genuinely sequence-space statement with no counterpart in the correlation framework. If anyone can apply it — connect it, or show the connection is not there — I would like to know. I have not been able to settle that, and it decides how much of the amplitude law is actually new.</p>
<p>The measurements behind the question are these. On a replication block of freshly generated zeros (n = 2000–2699), a demeaned AR(20) model improves held-out mean squared error by 85.0% over the mean baseline, while the identical pipeline run on <span class="math-container">$\beta$</span>-Hermite random-matrix surrogates, which set the generic repulsion floor, improves it by only 11 to 15%.</p>
<p>A ten-prime sinusoid whose amplitudes are fixed entirely by the explicit formula, with no fitted parameters, improves held-out error by 85.2%, against 65.5% for AR(20) on the same split (a different block from the replication above), and all ten measured amplitudes agree with the parameter-free prediction to within 13.3%. Across 200 shuffled nulls, no null draw reaches any observed amplitude (empirical p below 0.005 per prime), a result corroborated 0 out of 64 by an independent implementation, and nine decoy frequencies sit at null level. The ratio of measured amplitude to the null runs 1.6 to 2.6 across the 200 seeds, with a forking-paths count of 1.</p>
<p>If the prime component is removed, AR(20) on the residuals falls to 27.8%, at the repulsion floor. Prime powers add measurably on top of the distinct primes, 7.7 percentage points in the high range and 8.8 in the low.</p>
<p>The mechanism is of course the explicit formula (von Mangoldt 1895; Guinand–Weil), and prime oscillations in the statistics of the zeros are classical: Berry's 1988 semiclassical formula for the number variance, checked against Odlyzko's data; Bogomolny and Keating, Nonlinearity 8 (1995), 1115–1131, and 9 (1996), 911–935; Berry and Keating, SIAM Review 41 (1999), 236–266. Adjacent-gap dependence has been documented recently (Nishigaki 2025, arXiv:2507.10193), and the zeros have been machine-learned without any mechanism attached (Kampe and Vysogorets 2018).</p>
<p>What I am claiming is only the sequence-space package above. The composition of the remaining roughly 49% of the effect is open. No claim about the Riemann hypothesis is made. The primes have been expected in the zeros since 1859; this is a way of measuring them there, not a step toward a proof.</p>
<p>The computations were audited independently before this was posted, and the records are available on request. The data and code are pinned by SHA-256 so the numbers can be checked:</p>
<p>gammas700_verified.npy — 0a29097f32a6b4fe9cb3a6787cd8c2586cdd04090261c8093016be58ea087fce</p>
<p>exp5c_zeros_v3.npy — a572ac75aab0f322b673dd91c5ec4ba4a296961c17a7afeb631cccf54384a494</p>
<p>exp5c_replication_v3.py — c7099c9a3b34eb8c0b7d7986ceba72bf4bb766a7eba9c61c3f00dc57e16d939a</p>
<p>exp5c_replication_v3.json — 4eeeb70f185c2d4c7fed07162c120523432a1f62dbde4acb0edd9bb046921986</p>
<p>audit_h1f_am3.py — 3216a6b66cf378af968ad4f5f53d25c9d4e7b022ddd14d8b96ed4d46d505cc78</p>
<p>audit_h1f_am3_v1.json — c9bc5d92989b019547a89b0e882ce55421b14810ae43de7954623dd7080bbf18</p>

            <p>Let <span class="math-container">$p_n$</span> denote the <span class="math-container">$n$</span>-th prime and <span class="math-container">$g_n=p_{n+1}-p_n$</span>. For all sufficiently large <span class="math-container">$n$</span>, the bound

<p>What is the strongest known unconditional bound of the form <span class="math-container">$g_n\ll p_n^\theta$</span>? Is any <span class="math-container">$\theta&lt;1/2$</span> known?         <published>2026-10-23T21:37:21Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-26T20:53:57Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>In his essay <em><a href="https://www.dpmms.cam.ac.uk/%7Ewtg10/2cultures.pdf" rel="nofollow noreferrer">The Two Cultures of Mathematics</a></em>, Timothy Gowers distinguishes between <em>problem-solvers</em> and <em>theory-builders</em>.</p>
<p>Recent AI systems have demonstrated substantial progress in proving theorems and solving previously open mathematical problems. I am interested in a more specific type of mathematical contribution: the introduction of new concepts or structures that are useful beyond the original problem.</p>
<p><strong>Is there a documented example of an AI system introducing a mathematically nontrivial definition, invariant, construction, or abstract structure that was subsequently used to derive multiple results or establish a connection between previously separate problems?</strong></p>
<p>To make the question precise, I am looking for an example satisfying the following conditions:</p>
<ol>
<li>The mathematical object or concept was proposed by an AI system, rather than supplied to it by a human researcher.</li>
<li>Its definition and mathematical properties are explicitly documented in a publicly available paper or technical report.</li>
<li>Its usefulness is demonstrated by concrete mathematical results, rather than by a subjective assessment of its novelty or elegance.</li>
</ol>
<p>I am not asking whether AI will eventually become capable of developing mathematical theories, nor whether AI-generated mathematics is as creative as human mathematics.</p>
<p>I am looking for a verifiable example of AI contributing to the <em>conceptual development</em> of mathematics, rather than exclusively proving statements formulated in advance.</p>
<p>References identifying both the AI-generated concept and the mathematical results obtained from it would be particularly helpful.</p>

        <id>https://mathoverflow.net/q/514463</id>
        <re:rank scheme="https://mathoverflow.net">26</re:rank>
        <title type="text">Examples of problems that current AI models fail to solve but people can</title>
            <category scheme="https://mathoverflow.net/tags" term="big-list" />
            <category scheme="https://mathoverflow.net/tags" term="artificial-intelligence" />
        <author>
            <name>Gro-Tsen</name>
            <uri>https://mathoverflow.net/users/17064</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://mathoverflow.net/questions/514463/examples-of-problems-that-current-ai-models-fail-to-solve-but-people-can" />
        <published>2026-08-19T16:35:56Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-26T21:45:16Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p><strong>Important preliminary note</strong> (added 2026-08-19T23:58+02:00): The comments below show (and the downvotes probably suggest) that various people have interpreted my question as some combination of ⓐ representing problem-solving as a “humans versus AI” game, ⓑ wishing to either demonstrate human superiority in this matter or on the contrary to help improve AIs, and/or lastly ⓒ reducing mathematical practice to problem-solving.  <em>These three interpretations are all incorrect</em> (I can point to lengthy threads of mine on other social media to prove this, but I don't think MathOverflow is the appropriate place to discuss this).  The point of the question is to get a slightly less observation-biased understanding of what LLMs, in their current status, can and cannot do: we have enormous amounts of data about the “can”, so I'm trying to get some grasp on the “cannot” (and comparison with human beings is a natural point of reference because that is how we conceive of “difficulty”): this is in no way to be taken to be taken as any subjective judgement on my part about humans-versus-AI, or problem-solving, or anything of the sort.</p>
<p><strong>Another clarification</strong> (added 2026-08-20T13:42+02:00): Several people have worried in the comment that “AI fails to solve problem <span class="math-container">$X$</span>” is not a reproducible fact.  So, to be clear, I am <strong>not</strong> asking for examples where the LLM fails <em>reproducibly and systematically</em> to solve the problem — if it fails under reasonable conditions (i.e., at least one reasonably state-of-the-art model fails when given a reasonable amount of time), this qualifies as an example: please exercise your own judgment in what “reasonable”.  The same applies to the counterpart: I am not requiring that <em>each and every</em> person with knowledge in the field is able to solve the problem, only that we have reasonable suspicion that an averagely competent mathematician can solve it — again, exercise your own good faith judgment in deciding what this means.  Something like: “I tried asking [model] to prove [lemma], it failed, and I later realized it wasn't hard at all” is completely acceptable.</p>
<hr />
<p><strong>Background and motivation:</strong> There is now a <a href="https://mathoverflow.net/questions/502120/examples-for-the-use-of-ai-and-especially-llms-in-major-mathematical-development">long list of problems</a>, including many long-standing conjectures, that have been solved autonomously with current AI models.  The problem with this sort of list is that it conveys the idea that LLMs are now far better than human beings at problem-solving because they are able to solve many problems that people couldn't: while the conclusion <em>might</em> be correct, the reasoning certainly is not: it might also be the case that problem solving difficulty for LLMs and human brains is not well-correlated, and selecting problems hard for human beings still leaves a lot of problems that are easy for AI (selection bias).</p>
<p>Underlying this is also the <em>huge</em> observation bias that “AI model solves long-standing conjecture” is considered newsworthy and attentionworthy whereas “AI model fails to solve problem that turns out to be not that difficult after all” won't get reported.  There is the additional difficulty that any problem previously solved by people is probably already in the AI models' training set.</p>
<p>(I am aware of the <a href="https://1stproof.org/" rel="noreferrer"><em>First Proof</em> project</a> which seeks to confront this observation bias in a more scientific way, but I think it is still interesting to gather anecdotal evidence to put the positive AI news into perspective.)</p>
<p>Anyway, if we are to navigate this brave new world that has such AI in't, we need to understand its abilities in the sense of getting some kind of lower <em>and upper</em> estimates.  Now obviously there are some problems that current LLMs still can't solve: we know for theoretical reasons that there always will be, but we also know this more constructively because if someone had gotten their favorite model to solve one of the millennium problems, we would almost certainly have heard them boasting all over the Internet as if they had been part of the achievement: so by a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Adventure_of_Silver_Blaze" rel="noreferrer">“dog that didn't bark”</a> argument, I conclude that such problems are currently (still) out of reach of even the best LLMs that OpenAI, Anthropic &amp;co can make internally.</p>
<p>Still, I suspect that the upper bound can be improved beyond “ChatGPT can't solve the Riemann hypothesis”.  In fact, I suspect that problems still exist that mathematicians can solve with relative ease and LLMs can't, even if they maybe have to be constructed in a somewhat “adversarial” way: not so long ago, after all, some of the best models failed to accurately count the number of ‘r’s in “strawberry” or answer the question of whether there is <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W2xZxYaGlfs" rel="noreferrer">a seahorse emoji</a>: these examples can be attributed to oddities in the way LLMs work, but I see no reason why there shouldn't be such oddities within mathematics (e.g., maybe a conclusipn that can be easily seen by drawing a picture can be very hard for an LLM to reach).</p>
<p>Anyway:</p>
<p><strong>Question:</strong> Are there known examples of math problems that even the best current AI models fail to solve in a reasonable amount of time (or solve incorrectly) without human assistance, and which average specialist-in-the-field mathematicians can solve without AI assistance?</p>

        </summary>

        <published>2025-01-15T16:24:03Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-26T13:37:11Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p><strong>Main Question</strong></p>
<p>Suppose <span class="math-container">$f, g \in \mathbb{R}[x,y]$</span>, <span class="math-container">$\deg(f) &gt; \deg(g)$</span>, and their varieties in <span class="math-container">$\mathbb{R}^2$</span> satisfy <span class="math-container">$V(f) \subseteq V(g)$</span>. Must there also be <span class="math-container">$h \in \mathbb{R}[x,y]$</span> with <span class="math-container">$\deg(f) &gt; \deg(h)$</span> such that <span class="math-container">$$V(f)=V(g)\cap V(h)\,?$$</span></p>
<p>Does anyone have a proof or counterexample? There's a test case with a possible counterexample at the end.</p>
<p><strong>Motivating Example</strong></p>
<p>For polynomials of the form
<span class="math-container">$$f=p^2+q^2,\ \ g=p$$</span>
we can take
<span class="math-container">$$h=q.$$</span>
Loosely, this specifies the rest of <span class="math-container">$f$</span> after we know <span class="math-container">$g$</span>.</p>
<p><strong>Other (overlapping) examples</strong></p>
<p><span class="math-container">\begin{array}{ccc}
f &amp; g &amp; h\\
\hline
p^3 &amp; pr &amp; p\\
(p^{2a}+q^{2b})r^c &amp; pr &amp; qr\\
p^2(p^2+s^2+t^2)+q^2 &amp; p &amp; q\\
(p^2+q^2)(p^2+r^2) &amp; p &amp; qr\\
(p^2+q^2)(r^2+s^2) &amp; pr-qs &amp; ps+qr\\
p^2q^2+q^2r^2+r^2p^2 &amp; pqr &amp; \text{curve}
\end{array}</span>
with a curve going through the intersections <span class="math-container">$V(p)\cap V(q)$</span>, <span class="math-container">$V(q)\cap V(r)$</span> and <span class="math-container">$V(r)\cap V(p)$</span>.</p>
<p>In the last example, if <span class="math-container">$p=x$</span>, <span class="math-container">$\,q=y$</span> and <span class="math-container">$r=x+y-1$</span>, then <span class="math-container">$h=x^2-x+y^2-y$</span> works.</p>
<p><strong>Tempting Approach</strong></p>
<p>A tempting approach is defining <span class="math-container">$h$</span> as the remainder <span class="math-container">$f-f_1g$</span>, but this may not reduce the degree for bivariate polynomials. In the last example with <span class="math-container">$p,q,r$</span> as above, any <span class="math-container">$h$</span> of the form <span class="math-container">$f-f_1g$</span> will be at least quartic, and the intended <span class="math-container">$h$</span> does not seem to arise as a remainder. So this approach does not seem to work.</p>
<p><strong>Test case</strong></p>
<p>Suppose
<span class="math-container">$$f=(x^3-x)^2+(y(x-y+2)(x+y+2))^2$$</span>
<span class="math-container">$$g=(2x-y+1)(3x+y)(4x^2+x y+y^2-4)$$</span>
Then <span class="math-container">$f$</span> is sextic and <span class="math-container">$g$</span> is quartic -- is there a quintic <span class="math-container">$h$</span>?</p>
<p>On the <a href="https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i=graph%20of%20x%5E3-x%3D0%2C%20y%28x-y%2B2%29%28x%2By%2B2%29%3D0%2C%20%282x-y%2B1%29%283x%2By%29%284x%5E2%2Bx%20y%2By%5E2-4%29%3D0%20on%20x%3D-2..2%2C%20y%3D-3..3" rel="nofollow noreferrer">graph</a>, this is asking for a (red) quintic which intersects the green curves at exactly the nine points of the blue-and-orange grid.</p>
<p><a href="https://i.sstatic.net/it4aakwj.gif" rel="nofollow noreferrer"><img src="https://i.sstatic.net/it4aakwj.gif" alt="enter image description here" /></a></p>
<p>Since the blue and orange lines all intersect the green curves at points off the grid, none of them can be factors of the desired red curve.</p>

        <summary type="html">
            <p>Can you describe, in parametric form or in any other explicit way, all rational solutions to any of the following equations:
<span class="math-container">$$
y^2 + z^2 = x^3+1,
$$</span>
<span class="math-container">$$
y^2 + z^2 = x^3-1,
$$</span>
<span class="math-container">$$
y^2+x^2y+z^2+1=0.
$$</span>

<p>For the first two equations, I earlier asked the same question for integer solutions, see <a href="https://mathoverflow.net/questions/415173">How to describe all integer solutions to $x^2+y^2=z^3+1$?</a> , and no way more explicit than try all <span class="math-container">$x$</span> and solve the resulting equation in <span class="math-container">$(y,z)$</span> has been suggested. <p>The last equation has no integer solutions, but has rational ones.</p>
<p>The motivation for this question is that there three equations are the smallest ones (in a sense defined here: <a href="https://mathoverflow.net/questions/316708">What is the smallest unsolved Diophantine equation?</a>) for which the problem of describing all rational solutions is non-trivial.</p>
<p>Of course, the problem is equivalent to describing all coprime integers (or all integers, or all rationals) solutions to the homogeneous equations
<span class="math-container">$$
y^2t + z^2t = x^3+t^3,
$$</span>
<span class="math-container">$$
y^2t + z^2t = x^3-t^3,
$$</span>
<span class="math-container">$$
y^2t+x^2y+z^2t+t^3=0,
$$</span>
respectively.</p>

        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://mathoverflow.net/questions/365387/time-saving-technology-tricks-for-writing-papers" />
        <published>2020-07-11T09:10:16Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-26T13:16:29Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>I have over the years learned some tricks which saves a lot of time,
and I wish I had known them earlier. Some tricks are LaTeX-specific, but other tricks are more general. Let me start with a few examples:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Use LaTeX macros and definitions for easy reuse. This is particularly useful for when making many similar-looking figures. Another example is to make a macro that includes the <span class="math-container">$q$</span> when typing q-binomial coefficients. This ensures consistency.</p>
</li>
<li><p>In documents with many Tikz figures, compilation time can become quite brutal. However, spreading out all figures in many documents is also inconvenient. Solution: Use one standalone file, where each figure appears as a separate .pdf page. Then include the .pdf pages as figures in the main document. All figures are in one .tex-file, making it easy to reuse macros. <em>I find this trick extremely useful</em>, as it does not lead to duplicate code spread over several files.</p>
</li>
<li><p>Use bibtex and .bib files. I prefer to use <a href="https://www.doi2bib.org/" rel="noreferrer">doi2bib</a> to convert doi's to a .bib entry (some light editing might be needed).</p>
</li>
<li><p>For collaboration, use <em>git</em>. Also, Dropbox or similar for backups. Keeping track of versions has saved me several times.</p>
</li>
<li><p>Learn Regular expressions, for search-and-replace in .tex files. This is useful for converting hard-coded syntax into macros.</p>
</li>
<li><p>Get electronic (local) copies of standard references, and <em>make sure to name them in a sane manner</em>. Then it is easy to quickly search for the correct book. These are available when the wifi is down, or while traveling.</p>
</li>
<li><p>Do file reorganization and cleanup regularly. Get final versions of your published papers, and store in a folder, as you'll need them for job applications. Hunting down (your own!) published papers in pay-walled journals can be surprisingly tedious!</p>
</li>
<li><p>Take the time to move code snippets from project-specific notebooks, and turn into software packages for easy reuse. Also, it is sometimes worth to spend time optimizing code - waiting for code to run does not seem like a big deal, but I have noticed that small improvements in my work-flow can have big impact. I am much more likely to try out a conjecture if it is easy to run the code.</p>
</li>
</ul>

        </summary>

        <updated>2026-10-26T11:37:12Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>Let $W=\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty S_n$ be the union of all symmetric groups $S_n$. For an element $w\in W$, denote by $\mathfrak{S}_w$ the Schubert polynomial associated to $w$, and by $\partial_w$ the divided difference operator associated to $w$.</p>

<p><strong>Question:</strong> Let $u,v\in W$. Why is 
$$
\partial_u(\mathfrak{S}_u\mathfrak{S}_v)-\mathfrak{S}_v
$$
always a positive polynomial, in the sense that all coefficients are non-negative integers?</p>

<p><strong>Preliminary thoughts:</strong></p>

<ul>
<li><p>It is clear that $\partial_u(\mathfrak{S}_u\mathfrak{S}_v)$ is positive.</p></li>
<li><p>One may use the twisted Leipniz rule and induction on the length of $u$ to reduce the problem to an apparently simpler one. Indeed, let $s_i$ be the rightmost factor in a reduced expression of $u$. Then it suffices to show that $\partial_{us_i}(s_i\mathfrak{S}_u\partial_i\mathfrak{S}_v)$ is positive. (Here, $W$ acts on $\mathbb{Z}[x_1,x_2,x_3,\ldots]$ by permuting the variables.)</p></li>
<li><p>I was thinking to realize the polynomials in question as characters of representations, in the spirit of the work of M. Watanabe on KP modules, but had not much success.</p></li>
</ul>

<p>Any help would be greatly appreciated. I computed many examples and cannot find a counter example. In fact, I have a stronger "positivity conjecture" which implies this one, and even to this stronger conjecture, I was not able to find neither a counterexample nor a proof.</p>

        <title type="text">Is the class of inverse semigroups globally determined?</title>
            <category scheme="https://mathoverflow.net/tags" term="semigroups-and-monoids" />
            <category scheme="https://mathoverflow.net/tags" term="ra.rings-and-algebras" />
        <author>
            <name>Michał Masny</name>
            <uri>https://mathoverflow.net/users/20803</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://mathoverflow.net/questions/95575/is-the-class-of-inverse-semigroups-globally-determined" />
        <published>2012-04-30T13:50:03Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-26T23:47:29Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>This question is a follow-up to <a href="https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/101045/what-can-we-learn-about-a-group-by-studying-its-monoid-of-subsets">this one</a> I asked on math.stackexchange. I've decided to ask here because I believe this is a research-level question. I'm sorry if I'm wrong -- I'm not a researcher myself and may well be mistaken about it.</p>

<p>I will reitarate the definitions I posted in an answer to that question. For a semigroup $S,$ the set $\mathcal P (S)=2^S\setminus \lbrace \emptyset\rbrace$ with mutliplication given by $$AB=\lbrace ab\ |\ a\in A,b\in B\rbrace$$ is called the power semigroup of $S$. (I don't really know what removing the empty set from it makes any better, but this is what I found in most papers.) We say that two semigroups are globally isomorphic iff their power semigroups are isomorphic. We say that a class of semigroups $\mathscr C$ is globally determined iff any two globally isomorphic semigroups in $\mathscr C$ are automatically isomorphic, ie. for any $S,T\in\mathscr C$ we have $$\mathcal P(S)\cong\mathcal P(T)\implies S\cong T$$</p>

<p>The question I've linked to was about the class of all groups. As Steve D kindly pointed out in his answer, it is actually very simple to see that the class of all groups is globally determined. I started wondering if we can generalize this fact to all inverse semigroups, but in vain. There is little literature on this, even if I said otherwise previously. (I then meant that there was more than I'd expected.) Also, it seems to me that about 1990 papers on these things stopped appearing completely. Some that I've found are referenced on the linked page.</p>

        </summary>

        <title type="text">Fair but irregular polyhedral dice</title>
            <category scheme="https://mathoverflow.net/tags" term="mg.metric-geometry" />
            <category scheme="https://mathoverflow.net/tags" term="convex-polytopes" />
            <category scheme="https://mathoverflow.net/tags" term="recreational-mathematics" />

        <author>
            <name>Joseph O'Rourke</name>
            <uri>https://mathoverflow.net/users/6094</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://mathoverflow.net/questions/46684/fair-but-irregular-polyhedral-dice" />
        <published>2010-11-19T22:12:43Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-26T22:54:02Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>I am interested in determining a collection of geometric conditions that will guarantee that a convex polyhedron
of $n$ faces is a <em>fair die</em> in the sense that, upon random rolling, it has an equal $1/n$ probability of
landing on each of its faces.
(Assume the polyhedron is composed of a homogeneous material; i.e., it is not "loaded.")</p>

<p>There has been study of what Grünbaum and Shephard call <em>isohedral</em> polyhedra,
which always represent fair dice: "An <a href="http://mathworld.wolfram.com/Isohedron.html" rel="noreferrer">isohedron</a> is a convex polyhedron with symmetries acting transitively on its faces with respect to the center of gravity. Every isohedron has an even number of faces."
It is clear such a polyhedral die is fair.
Here is an example of the <em>trapezoidal dodecahedron</em>, an isohedron of 12 congruent faces,
from <a href="http://www.aleakybos.ch/Shapes.htm" rel="noreferrer">an attractive web site on polyhedral dice</a>:
<br />
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<img src="https://i.sstatic.net/uEZdf.jpg" alt="trapezoidal dodecahedron">
<br />
But a clever argument in a delightful paper
by Persi Diaconis and Joseph Keller
("<a href="http://www-stat.stanford.edu/~cgates/PERSI/papers/fairdice.pdf" rel="noreferrer">Fair Dice</a>." <em>Amer. Math. Monthly</em> 96, 337-339, 1989)
shows (essentially, by continuity) that there must be fair polyhedral dice 
that are not symmetric.
For example, there is no reason to expect that equal face areas is a necessary condition
for a polyhedral die to be fair.
Nor is it reasonable to expect that the distance from each face to the center of gravity
of the polyhedron is alone a determining condition. 
Rather it should depend on the dihedral angles between faces, the likelihood of one face
rolling to the next&mdash;perhaps a <a href="http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain" rel="noreferrer">Markov chain</a> of transitions?</p>

<p>My question is:</p>

<blockquote>
  <p>Is there a collection of geometric conditions&mdash;broader than isohedral&mdash;that guarantee
  that a (perhaps asymetrical, perhaps unequal-face-areas) convex polyhedron represents
  a fair die?</p>
</blockquote>

<p>Sufficient conditions welcomed; necessary and sufficient conditions may be too much to hope for!
Speculations and literature leads appreciated!</p>

        </summary>
    </entry>

        <summary type="html">
            <p>I am attempting to find a closed form solution or a nice series for $x^{x+1}=(x+1)^{x}$.  First of all I looked at $a^b=b^a$. Fixing a, this means finding out when $a^{1/a} = x^{1/x}$. $f(x)=x^{1/x}$ is an interesting function. It has a maximum at e. (Proof due to Jakub Steiner.) $x^{1/x}$ goes to 1 as x goes to infinity. Based on that, I can conclude that $a^{1/a} = x^{1/x}$ has non-trivial solutions when x > 1 and that when a > e the non-trivial solution is between 1 and $e^{1/e}$.</p>

<p>I thought this was pretty neat, but it isn't helping me to solve the original problem. So, I would like to know is there a name, given a, for the value of b (not equal to a) such that $a^b = b^a$? For example, we could call b the "switch-ponent" of a but there must be a better name than that. Anyone know what these are called or maybe a name for the original problem?</p>

        </summary>
